content: White spirit, also referred to as Stoddard solvent, is a clear and transparent liquid derived from paraffin. It is widely used as an organic solvent in painting and decorating applications. In 1924, W.J. Stoddard, a dry cleaner from Atlanta, collaborated with Lloyd E. Jackson of the Mellon Research Institute to create specifications for a less volatile dry-cleaning solvent as an alternative to the more volatile petroleum-based solvents. By 1928, dry cleaners began using this solvent, and it became the predominant dry-cleaning solvent in the United States from the late 1920s until the late 1950s. White spirit is a mixture of saturated aliphatic and alicyclic hydrocarbons with carbon chains ranging from C7 to C12. It can contain up to 25% of C7 to C12 alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons. Its applications include use as an extraction solvent, a cleaning solvent, a degreasing agent, and as a solvent in products such as aerosols, paints, wood preservatives, lacquers, varnishes, and asphalt products. In Western Europe, approximately 60% of white spirit consumption is attributed to its use in paints, lacquers, and varnishes, making it the most widely used solvent in the paint industry. In households, it is commonly employed to clean paintbrushes after decorating, as its paint-thinning properties prevent paint from hardening and damaging the bristles, allowing brushes to be reused. There are three types and three grades of white spirit. The type is determined by the treatment process: Type 1 undergoes hydrodesulfurization (removal of sulfur), Type 2 involves solvent extraction, and Type 3 is subjected to hydrogenation. Each type is further divided into three grades: low flash grade, regular grade, and high flash grade. The grade depends on the crude oil used as the starting material and the distillation conditions. Additionally, there is a Type 0, which is defined as a distillation fraction with no further treatment, consisting predominantly of saturated C9 to C12 hydrocarbons with a boiling range of 140–200°C. Physical Properties The physical properties of the three types of white spirit vary depending on their composition and treatment process. Toxicity White spirit is primarily classified as an irritant. It has relatively low acute toxicity when inhaled as vapor, absorbed through the skin, or ingested. However, acute exposure can depress the central nervous system, leading to symptoms such as impaired coordination, slowed reactions, and, in severe cases, unconsciousness. Oral ingestion poses a significant aspiration hazard. Prolonged or repeated skin exposure over time can result in severe irritant dermatitis, also known as contact dermatitis. To minimize skin exposure, it is strongly recommended to use gloves and wash hands after contact. Occasional skin exposure is unlikely to cause significant issues. Chronic exposure to white spirit at concentrations of 240 mg/m³ (40 ppm) for more than 13 years has been associated with chronic central nervous system effects. It has also been implicated in the development of chronic toxic encephalopathy among house painters. Despite its moderate toxicity to aquatic organisms, white spirit is unlikely to pose significant environmental hazards due to the volatility and low bioavailability of its constituents. However, it should not be intentionally poured down sinks or freshwater drains. Proper disposal methods should be followed whenever possible.
